meta.house_style: Each objective carries three steps to success (child-friendly, I can) and one challenge. Maths and Science done from White Rose. English and IPC follow once the house style is confirmed; the engine produces the same three plus challenge on every generated lesson.
meta.suggested_note: Steps to success and misconceptions for Writing, Reading and IPC are SEQUENS-suggested, not from a scheme. Maths and Science come from White Rose. The engine confirms the real hinge at generation; you confirm the rest.

english.subject: English
english.eua: End of Unit Assessment: Writing independently (narrative). The year is 2055; you are a space scientist on Mars stranded on a probe with your partner Auggie. Tell the story of the day, describe the Mars landscape, how you get stuck, the dialogue that reveals who Auggie is and how it makes you feel, and the rescue. Sits at Week 7 Lesson 5.

objectives.objective: To analyze how an author uses language choices to create a tense atmospheric narrative opening.
success: I can keep a consistent tense.
I can use the perfect and progressive forms.
I can check my tense across paragraphs.
objectives.hinge: Slips between tenses within the piece.

objectives.objective: To use precise expanded noun phrases to describe the physical details of a setting.
success: I can build a noun phrase that adds detail.
I can choose words that carry meaning, not just decoration.
I can check the phrase helps the reader picture it.
objectives.hinge: Piles on adjectives without the phrase adding real information.

objectives.objective: To use fronted adverbials to establish context, time, and place in a setting description.
success: I can start a sentence with an adverbial.
I can put the comma in the right place.
I can vary where I place it for effect.
objectives.hinge: Forgets the comma after the fronted adverbial.

objectives.objective: To select and apply figurative language devices (similes and metaphors) to enhance narrative imagery.
success: I can write a simile or metaphor.
I can make it fit the mood of the writing.
I can check it adds to the image, not just decorates.
objectives.hinge: Writes a simile that decorates but does not deepen the image.

objectives.objective: To construct a cohesive narrative opening paragraph that establishes an immersive setting.
success: I can link ideas across sentences.
I can vary my cohesive devices.
I can keep the writing flowing across paragraphs.
objectives.hinge: Repeats the same connective instead of varying the cohesion.

1.gps: Parts of speech and rules of punctuation revision.

objectives.objective: To analyze how a character is introduced through a unique, controlled narrative perspective.
success: I can write in a consistent voice.
I can keep the perspective steady.
I can make the voice sound authentic.
objectives.hinge: Loses the character's voice partway through.

objectives.objective: To develop and maintain a consistent, authentic first-person narrative voice.
success: I can write in a consistent voice.
I can keep the perspective steady.
I can make the voice sound authentic.
objectives.hinge: Loses the character's voice partway through.

objectives.objective: To show character traits and feelings through internal thoughts and physical actions rather than telling.
success: I can understand what the task asks.
I can write to meet it.
I can check my writing against the criteria.
objectives.hinge: Writes to the task without checking it against the success criteria.

objectives.objective: To use relative clauses (who, which, whose, that) to add depth and precision when describing secondary characters.
success: I can add a relative clause with who, which, whose or that.
I can punctuate it correctly.
I can use it to add useful detail.
objectives.hinge: Drops or misplaces the commas, or uses the wrong relative pronoun.

2.gps: Revision of types of sentences (simple, compound and complex).

objectives.objective: To identify key plot milestones in a novel and explore how an author builds internal conflict.
success: I can understand what the task asks.
I can write to meet it.
I can check my writing against the criteria.
objectives.hinge: Writes to the task without checking it against the success criteria.

objectives.objective: To draft a structured character-focused paragraph introducing a key protagonist.
success: I can organise my writing into paragraphs.
I can start a new one when the focus shifts.
I can link paragraphs together.
objectives.hinge: Starts a new paragraph in the wrong place.

objectives.objective: To punctuate direct speech accurately to create realistic dialogue between characters.
success: I can punctuate direct speech correctly.
I can start a new line for a new speaker.
I can use dialogue to show character.
objectives.hinge: Puts the comma or full stop outside the speech marks.

objectives.objective: To integrate dialogue within a scene to reveal character betrayals and shift relationships.
success: I can punctuate direct speech correctly.
I can start a new line for a new speaker.
I can use dialogue to show character.
objectives.hinge: Puts the comma or full stop outside the speech marks.

objectives.objective: To use active and passive voice deliberately to alter emphasis during a high-stakes conflict scene.
success: I can tell active from passive voice.
I can choose the one that suits my emphasis.
I can explain why I chose it.
objectives.hinge: Shifts between active and passive without a purpose.

3.gps: Creating atmosphere, and integrating dialogue (revision of punctuation) to convey character and advance action and engage audience in writing.

objectives.objective: To vary sentence lengths and clause structures to control pacing and escalate dramatic tension.
success: I can vary my sentence lengths.
I can use short sentences for tension.
I can control the pace of the scene.
objectives.hinge: Uses only long sentences, so tension is flat.

objectives.objective: To analyze structural narrative endings and draft a resolution where characters learn a lesson about empathy.
success: I can organise my writing into paragraphs.
I can start a new one when the focus shifts.
I can link paragraphs together.
objectives.hinge: Starts a new paragraph in the wrong place.

objectives.objective: To use advanced punctuation (colons, semi-colons, dashes, and brackets) to add parenthesis or mark boundaries between independent clauses.
success: I can use a colon, semicolon or brackets.
I can put them where they belong.
I can check they make the meaning clearer.

objectives.objective: To apply conjunctive adverbials and structural cohesive devices to link ideas smoothly across narrative paragraphs.
success: I can link ideas across sentences.
I can vary my cohesive devices.
I can keep the writing flowing across paragraphs.
objectives.hinge: Repeats the same connective instead of varying the cohesion.

objectives.objective: To evaluate, refine, edit, and proofread a narrative scene draft for sentence fluency and grammatical accuracy.
success: I can reread for meaning.
I can edit for flow and accuracy.
I can proofread for punctuation and spelling.
objectives.hinge: Only fixes spelling and misses meaning and flow.

4.gps: Using a range of cohesive devices, including adverbials, within and across sentences and paragraphs.

objectives.objective: To identify the audience, purpose, and layout features of a formal recount text or diary shift.
success: I can write in a formal register.
I can avoid casual words.
I can match the tone to the purpose.

success: I can keep a consistent tense.
I can use the perfect and progressive forms.
I can check my tense across paragraphs.

success: I can tell active from passive voice.
I can choose the one that suits my emphasis.
I can explain why I chose it.
objectives.hinge: Shifts between active and passive without a purpose.

objectives.objective: To use bullet points and colons correctly to introduce a formal list of rules or precepts.
success: I can use a colon, semicolon or brackets.
I can put them where they belong.
I can check they make the meaning clearer.
objectives.hinge: Uses advanced punctuation in the wrong place.

objectives.objective: To plan an explanation text breaking down the deeper moral meaning behind a formal precept.
success: I can plan the shape of my writing.
I can order my ideas.

objectives.hinge: Plans as a list of events with no shape.

objectives.objective: To draft a formal explanation text using cohesive devices to link ideas smoothly across distinct paragraph blocks.
success: I can link ideas across sentences.
I can vary my cohesive devices.
I can keep the writing flowing across paragraphs.
objectives.hinge: Repeats the same connective instead of varying the cohesion.

objectives.objective: To identify the key features and persuasive techniques used to champion a social cause.
success: I can state a clear viewpoint.
I can support it with reasons.
I can use persuasive techniques.

success: I can use modal verbs and adverbs of possibility.
I can pick ones that add authority.
I can match the strength to my point.

success: I can write in a formal register.
I can avoid casual words.
I can match the tone to the purpose.

ipc.subject: IPC
ipc.unit: 900 CE: The Mayan Civilisation, Civilisation of West Africa
ipc.exit_point: Execute a comparative civilisation synthesis block, presenting ancient regional outcomes.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: Entry Point & Timeline: Construct a regional timeline focusing on global civilisations around 900 CE.
success: I can place events in time order.
I can compare when things happened.
I can avoid judging the past as primitive.
lessons.hinge: Thinks older civilisations were simpler or less advanced.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: Knowledge Harvest: Gauge baseline student vocabulary regarding ancient history, archaeology, and chronology.
success: I can place events in time order.
I can compare when things happened.
I can avoid judging the past as primitive.
lessons.hinge: Thinks older civilisations were simpler or less advanced.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: History (3.01): Formulate inquiry questions related to different geographic perspectives of Mesoamerica around 900 CE.
success: I can ask a geographical question.
I can look at more than one source.
I can weigh what each tells me.
lessons.hinge: Treats one map or source as the whole truth.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: History (3.05): Identify the geographical features, infrastructure, and city-state layouts of the Maya civilization.
success: I can describe the features of a Maya city.
I can explain how it was organised.
I can use evidence for my description.
lessons.hinge: Assumes ancient cities had no planning or scale.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: History (3.04): Understand how historians build inferences about daily Mayan life based on archaeological artifacts.
success: I can describe an artefact.
I can infer what it suggests about daily life.
I can say how sure I am and why.
lessons.hinge: Treats an artefact as proof rather than evidence to interpret.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: History (3.05): Analyse social hierarchies, trade routes, and the roles of rulers vs. artisans within Maya society.
success: I can describe different roles in Maya society.
I can explain how they depended on each other.
I can use evidence for my ideas.
lessons.hinge: Assumes everyone in the past lived the same way.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: History (3.10): Evaluate how ancient Mayan ideas, agricultural methods, and beliefs have influenced modern societies.
success: I can find a Maya idea that lasted.
I can trace it to today.
I can explain the link.
lessons.hinge: Thinks nothing from 900 CE still matters today.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: Cultural Myths: Explore Mayan polytheism, ritual practices, and sacred mythology (e.g., the Popul Vuh).
success: I can retell a Maya myth.
I can explain what it meant to them.
I can tell belief apart from fact.
lessons.hinge: Confuses myth and belief with historical fact.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: History (3.11): Examine Mayan technological developments, tracking their sophisticated logographic writing system and codices.
success: I can describe the Maya writing system.
I can explain what it was used for.
I can compare it with writing today.
lessons.hinge: Assumes ancient people had no science or learning.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: Mathematical Advancements: Study the structural development of the Mayan base-20 numbering system and solar calendars.
success: I can read a Maya number.
I can explain the base-20 idea.
I can compare it with our system.
lessons.hinge: Thinks base-20 is just a wrong version of base-10.

lessons.objective: Lesson A: History (3.02 & 3.12): Analyse theories behind the Classic Maya collapse, evaluating how multiple causes contribute to changes in society.
success: I can name possible causes of the collapse.
I can explain how they interacted.
I can weigh which mattered most.
lessons.hinge: Looks for one single cause instead of several interacting ones.

lessons.objective: Exit point prep.
success: I can compare two civilisations.
I can use evidence for each.
I can present a fair conclusion.
lessons.hinge: Judges one civilisation as better rather than comparing fairly.

lessons.objective: Lesson B: Exit Point: Execute a comparative civilisation synthesis block, presenting ancient regional outcomes.
success: I can compare two civilisations.
I can use evidence for each.
I can present a fair conclusion.
lessons.hinge: Judges one civilisation as better rather than comparing fairly.

ipc.note: Weekly lessons are Maya-focused. West Africa is named in the unit title and appears only in the Exit Point comparative synthesis. The plan may be incomplete; left exactly as supplied, nothing invented.

science.subject: Science
science.source: White Rose Science, Year 6 Autumn Block 1
science.enquiry_question: How can animals, plants and microorganisms be identified, grouped and classified?
science.pacing_note: White Rose Science is written for content, not time. Mapped 1 small step per week (default). Confirm lessons per week.

steps.title: Conditions for life
steps.nc: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including microorganisms, plants and animals.
steps.ws: Identifying scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments.
success: I can name what living things need to survive.
I can explain why something is living or non-living.
I can sort things into living and non-living and say why.
steps.challenge: A plant does not run around like an animal. Is it living or non-living? Explain your answer using what a plant can do.

practical.objective: Collect living and non-living examples in the school grounds and justify each grouping.
practical.ws: Identifying scientific evidence used to support or refute ideas.
success: I can collect a range of living and non-living things.
I can group them and give a reason for each.
I can use evidence to defend a tricky case.
practical.challenge: Find one thing that is hard to call living or non-living, and argue both sides.

steps.title: Group organisms
steps.nc: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including microorganisms, plants and animals.
steps.ws: Use and develop keys and other information records to identify, classify and describe living things (non-statutory).
success: I can name the five vertebrate groups.
I can tell a flowering plant from a non-flowering plant.
I can group organisms in more than one way and explain my groups.
steps.challenge: A whale lives in the sea. Is it a fish? Explain how you know.

practical.objective: Sort images of plants and animals in more than one way and explain each grouping.
practical.ws: Use and develop keys and other records to identify and classify.
success: I can group organisms by a feature I choose.
I can regroup them a different way.
I can explain what each group has in common.
practical.challenge: Set a grouping puzzle for a partner and see if they can find your rule.

steps.title: Classify animals
steps.nc: Give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.
steps.ws: Use and develop keys and other information records to identify, classify and describe living things and materials, and identify patterns that might be found in the natural environment (non-statutory).
success: I can say what a classification key is and why we use it.
I can use yes and no questions to sort animals.
I can make my own classification key for a set of animals.
steps.challenge: Write three yes/no questions that would separate a spider, a snail and a beetle.

practical.objective: Build and test a classification key for a set of animals using yes and no questions.
practical.ws: Use and develop keys to identify, classify and describe living things.
success: I can write yes and no questions about features.
I can order them into a key.
I can test my key on a new animal.
practical.challenge: Trade keys with a group and find an animal that breaks theirs.

steps.title: Classify plants
steps.nc: Give reasons for classifying plants and animals based on specific characteristics.
steps.ws: Use and develop keys and other information records to identify, classify and describe living things and materials and identify patterns that might be found in the natural environment (non-statutory).
success: I can name features that help me classify plants.
I know what deciduous, evergreen and coniferous mean.
I can make a key to sort flowering and non-flowering plants.
steps.challenge: Someone says a mushroom is a plant because it has a stem. Are they right? Explain your answer.

practical.objective: Create and compare classification keys for real plants and leaves.
practical.ws: Use and develop keys and identify patterns in the natural environment.
success: I can look closely at a plant's features.
I can build a key that separates the plants.
I can compare my key with another group's.
practical.challenge: Add a coniferous example and adjust your key to include it.

steps.title: Microorganisms
steps.nc: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including microorganisms, plants and animals.
steps.ws: Identifying scientific evidence that has been used to support or refute ideas or arguments.
success: I can name the three types of microorganism.
I can give an example of a helpful and a harmful microorganism.
I can explain why we need a microscope to see them.
steps.challenge: 'All bacteria are harmful.' Is this always, sometimes or never true? Explain.

practical.objective: Set up the mould-growth observation over time, a dry and a damp slice in sealed bags, and record the changes.
practical.ws: Observation over time; taking and recording measurements.
success: I can set up a dry and a damp sample fairly.
I can keep the bags sealed and safe.
I can record the mould changes over time.
practical.challenge: Predict which bag will change fastest and say why.

steps.title: Classify organisms
steps.nc: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including microorganisms, plants and animals.
steps.ws: Reporting and presenting findings from enquiries, including conclusions, causal relationships and explanations of and a degree of trust in results, in oral and written forms such as displays and other presentations.
success: I can explain that microorganisms can be classified by their features.
I can describe the shape of bacteria, viruses and fungi in simple words.
I can make a key to sort microorganisms.
steps.challenge: Play 'which microorganism am I?' Write the three yes/no questions you would ask to work it out.

practical.objective: Play 'which microorganism am I?' and build a key to sort bacteria, viruses and fungi.
practical.ws: Reporting and presenting findings from enquiries.
success: I can ask yes and no questions about shape and features.
I can sort the three types with a key.
I can present how I classified them.
practical.challenge: Explain why a virus is the hardest of the three to place, using its features.

steps.title: Carl Linnaeus
steps.nc: Describe how living things are classified into broad groups according to common observable characteristics and based on similarities and differences, including microorganisms, plants and animals.
steps.ws: Use relevant scientific language and illustrations to discuss, communicate and justify their ideas and should talk about how scientific ideas have developed over time (non-statutory).
success: I can say who Carl Linnaeus was and what he did.
I can explain why his system was not fully accurate.
I can describe how classification has changed since his time.
steps.challenge: Linnaeus did not know about microorganisms. How has science let us classify them since his time?

practical.objective: Research Linnaeus and produce a timeline and a short science-journalist article.
practical.ws: Talk about how scientific ideas have developed over time.
success: I can find key facts about Linnaeus and his system.
I can place them on a timeline.
I can explain why his system was not fully accurate.
practical.challenge: Explain how one modern discovery would have changed how Linnaeus grouped things.

science.model: Two 40-minute lessons a week: one White Rose small step and one practical in the science lab. Content coverage is one step a week; the practical carries the working-scientifically and enquiry strands.

maths.subject: Maths
maths.source: White Rose Maths, Year 6 Autumn Block 1
maths.unit: Place value, then Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division
maths.pacing_note: Autumn 1 runs Place value (this block, 8 steps) then Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. The second block's SOL was not supplied, so its steps are not mapped. Send the White Rose Year 6 Autumn Block 2 SOL and it will be mapped verbatim. Also set maths lessons per week so both blocks pace onto the teaching days.

steps.title: Numbers to 1,000,000
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can say what each digit is worth in a number up to 1,000,000.
I can build and partition a number in more than one way.
I can add or take away 10, 100, 1,000 or 10,000 and say which column changes.
steps.challenge: Annie has 4 ten-thousands, 12 thousands, 8 hundreds, 3 tens and 25 ones counters. What is the greatest number she can make?

steps.title: Numbers to 10,000,000
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can read a 7-digit number and say what each digit is worth.
I can put the commas in the right places in a 7-digit number.
I can show a number up to 10,000,000 on a place value chart.
steps.challenge: Jack has counters worth 1,000,000, 10,000 and 1. Using only four counters, what different numbers greater than 1,000,000 can he make?

steps.title: Read and write numbers to 10,000,000
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can write a large number in words.
I can write a large number in numerals when I am given the words.
I can use the commas to break a big number into parts to read it.
steps.challenge: Write 'three and a half million' in numerals. Then write 5,208,001 in words.

steps.title: Powers of 10
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1,000.
I can say how many times bigger or smaller one number is than another.
I know that multiplying by 10 twice is the same as multiplying by 100.
steps.challenge: Huan thinks a number a thousand times the size of 2,500 is two and a half million. Is Huan right? Explain how you know.

steps.title: Number line to 10,000,000
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can work out what each interval on a number line is worth.
I can find where a number belongs on a number line to 10,000,000.
I can find the midpoint between two numbers on the line.
steps.challenge: Tiny says the arrow points to 3,050,000 but it is halfway between 3 and 4 million. Explain the mistake Tiny has made.

steps.title: Compare and order any integers
steps.nc: Read, write, order and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can compare two numbers using the place value of their digits.
I can use the <, > and = signs correctly.
I can order a set of numbers from smallest to largest and back again.
steps.challenge: Explain why 56,700 is not greater than 201,000, even though 5 is greater than 2.

steps.title: Round any integer
steps.nc: Round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can find the two multiples a number sits between.
I can round a number to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 and million.
I can choose the most sensible way to round a number.
steps.challenge: My number rounds to 38,000 to the nearest thousand. What is the greatest it could be, and the smallest?

steps.title: Negative numbers
steps.nc: Use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across zero. Solve number and practical problems that involve the above.
success: I can read a temperature above and below zero.
I can count forwards and backwards through zero.
I can find the difference between a positive and a negative number.
steps.challenge: Harlow is -3 degrees and Southampton is 4 degrees. Find the difference. Then Bradford drops 6 degrees from 2 degrees. What is its new temperature?

pending_blocks.source: White Rose Maths, Year 6 Autumn Block 2

reading.subject: English Reading
reading.source: SEQUENS synthesis: VIPERS, Year 6 age-related expectations (reading domains 2a to 2h). Texts original and adjacent to Wonder.
reading.note: Not from a school scheme. Synthesised around VIPERS and the Year 6 reading content domains, with original texts written to sit alongside Wonder. Five lessons a week. Confirm or cut; nothing here is presented as El Alsson's curriculum.

lessons.objective: To work out the meaning of unfamiliar words in "The New Kid" using clues from the surrounding text.
success: I can find a word I do not know in the text.
I can use the words around it to work out what it means.
I can check my meaning makes sense in the sentence.
lessons.challenge: Find a word the writer could have used instead, and say how it would change the feeling of the sentence.
lessons.hinge: Guesses a word from how it looks instead of using the words around it.

lessons.objective: To retrieve and record key details from "The New Kid" and find the evidence that supports them.
success: I can find the answer to a question in the text.
I can point to the exact words that prove it.
I can write my answer in a full sentence.
lessons.challenge: Find a detail that is hinted at but not stated directly, and show the words that hint at it.
lessons.hinge: Answers from memory rather than finding the exact words in the text.

lessons.objective: To infer how a character feels in "The New Kid" and justify it with evidence.
success: I can say how a character is feeling.
I can find words or actions that show it.
I can explain how the evidence proves my idea.
lessons.challenge: Find two moments where the same character feels differently, and explain what changed.
lessons.hinge: Gives an opinion but no evidence from the text to back it.

lessons.objective: To predict what a character might do next in "The New Kid" and explain the word choices that point to it.
success: I can say what I think will happen next.
I can use clues from the text to back up my idea.
I can explain how a word or phrase points to what is coming.
lessons.challenge: Write two different predictions and say which one the text makes more likely, and why.
lessons.hinge: Predicts from imagination rather than from clues in the text.

lessons.objective: To summarise the main events of "The New Kid" in order and in my own words.
success: I can pick out the most important events.
I can put them in the right order.
I can retell the text in a few sentences of my own.
lessons.challenge: Summarise the text in exactly twenty words, keeping only what matters most.
lessons.hinge: Retells everything instead of choosing the main points.

lessons.objective: To work out the meaning of unfamiliar words in "Behind the Mask" using clues from the surrounding text.
